assessment: Full assembly plausibly offers an opportunity to detect missing parts and insertion trouble before dispatch, but its effectiveness is unmeasured. No damage claims were recorded (O7); this does not establish that full assembly prevented damage. The incumbent misses the observed time and unaided-arrangement targets (O2, O4). O6 limits an account of uniformly slow assembly: both workers completed repeated simple layouts in seven to nine minutes, while all extreme delays occurred in mixed batches. Layout complexity and switching remain confounded. O5 likewise limits a width-only explanation of reinsertion because measured widths overlap. Five partition complaints indicate a problem but do not establish five verified packing omissions.

openings.claim: Switching among order configurations may increase selection and checking time; grouping identical layouts could improve the incumbent without changing its assembly method.
openings.delta: Distinguishes switching overhead from inherently longer six-compartment assembly.
openings.prediction: For matched layouts and colors, grouped sequences reduce selection/checking time relative to mixed sequences; insertion time changes little if switching is the main cause.
openings.probe: Use reusable samples and both workers in a counterbalanced comparison of grouped and mixed sequences containing identical orders. Time selection, insertion, checking and packing separately; audit required parts and exterior color. Compare within layout and worker. Stop sampling before it threatens the fixed delivery date.
assumptions: A bounded comparison fits available working time.
Any adoption retains accepted counts, colors, footprint, capacity and removable partitions; total initial spending stays within 500 and added material cost within 0.40 per order.

openings.claim: Does short-partition confusion persist when contents are verified and the diagram shows only the ordered arrangement?
openings.delta: Separates diagram ambiguity from missing components or physical assembly difficulty.
openings.prediction: If diagram ambiguity contributes, an order-specific diagram reduces wrong placements and requests for help while insertion difficulty remains similar.
openings.probe: Give ten participants verified complete, matched organizers; assign five the existing diagram and five an order-specific diagram. Record unaided success, short-partition placement, help requests and insertion retries. Treat results as exploratory. Measure diagram preparation time and incremental cost before adoption.
assumptions: Matching and assignment sufficiently limit participant differences for an exploratory comparison.
Diagram substitution retains every physical specification and accepted order choice, fits the stated budget and does not delay delivery.
